error_modes.label: WINGMAN ANTICIPATION OF NO1 INTENTION WITHOUT ASSUMPTION

texts.0: SP, due to a mental model of the flight built on assumption instead of on the briefed contract, acted on what No1 was expected to do rather than on what No1 actually did. SP initiated a position change for a turn that had never been signalled and left the briefed position with no visual signal or radio call received. The resulting geometry produced an uncontrolled closure with lead and the IP took control to separate the aircraft. The remaining formation profile was terminated.
texts.1: SP, due to a mental model that filled the gaps with assumption rather than with confirmed information, repeatedly started position changes before No1 signal was identified. Each wrong anticipation was corrected only after direct verbal prompting by the IP. Position and spacing were restored late and the flight was reformed at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an incomplete check of No1 visual signals against the briefed sequence, began to anticipate the next maneuver on expectation rather than on a confirmed signal. SP recognized the error before the deviation developed, returned to the briefed position and held it until the signal was given. No IP input was required and formation geometry stayed clear of the standard limits.
texts.3: SP anticipated No1 intention from the briefed sequence, the flight profile and lead aircraft attitude, but acted only on a confirmed visual signal or radio call. Position changes were initiated at the correct point, and where the picture was ambiguous SP asked instead of assuming.
texts.4: SP stayed one step ahead of No1 throughout the sortie, correlating the briefed sequence, lead energy state and the visual signals so that every position change was prepared before it was ordered. No action was taken on assumption at any point and each ambiguity was resolved with a short standard call. Formation integrity was maintained without a single unrequested movement.
texts.marginal: SP anticipated No1 intention correctly and generally acted on confirmed signals, but twice started the movement on expectation and verified the signal only afterwards. The trend was toward assuming rather than confirming whenever the sequence felt familiar. SP is expected to keep the anticipation mental and to move only after the signal has been positively identified.

texts_at.0: SP practiced anticipating No1 with the IP calling the point to return to the briefed position when a move was started on assumption rather than a confirmed signal. Waiting for a confirmed signal before moving is still new at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin waiting for the confirmed signal without the IP's calls.
texts_at.1: SP returned to the briefed position and held it until the signal was given, though the return followed only once IP prompted verbally, with position and spacing restored late and the formation reformed at the limit of the acceptable standard. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to return to the briefed position without the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP anticipated the next maneuver from the briefed sequence, correcting without prompting the occasional move that had begun on expectation before the signal was confirmed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to complete the check of each visual signal against the briefed sequence before anticipating, so the early movement does not start.
texts_at.3: SP anticipated No1 intention correctly and generally acted on confirmed signals within standard, though twice the movement was started on expectation and the signal verified only afterwards, with a trend toward assuming rather than confirming whenever the sequence felt familiar. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep the anticipation mental and to move only after the signal has been positively identified.

texts_above.1: SP returned to the briefed position and held it until the signal was given, though the return first followed only once prompted, with position and spacing restored late. The return followed a verbal prompt from the IP. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP caught each early movement made on expectation before it developed, returned to the briefed position without prompting and held it until the signal was given, so formation geometry stayed clear of the standard limits. Completing the check of the signal against the briefed sequence before anticipating would remove the early movement entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good recovery of an anticipated maneuver before it developed into a deviation.
texts_above.3: SP anticipated No1 intention from the briefed sequence, the flight profile and lead aircraft attitude, but acted only on a confirmed visual signal or radio call, with position changes initiated at the correct point and, where the picture was ambiguous, asking instead of assuming. The only refinement left is to hold the same discipline into a sequence that departs from the briefed one. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good discipline in confirming before acting on an anticipated maneuver.
texts_above.4: SP stayed one step ahead of No1 throughout the sortie, correlating the briefed sequence, lead energy state and the visual signals so every position change was prepared before it was ordered, with no action taken on assumption at any point and each ambiguity resolved with a short standard call, keeping formation integrity intact without a single unrequested movement. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to excellent correlation of the briefed sequence with lead's actual signals.

error_modes.label: AWARENESS AND JUDGMENT - ORIENTATION AND CROSS-CHECK WHILE FLYING POSITION

texts.0: SP, due to a cross-check that stopped alternating between lead aircraft, own control and performance instruments and the outside references, lost track of the flight position relative to the field and the assigned area. Own altitude, airspeed and fuel state were left unmonitored while attention stayed on lead. The flight left the assigned area and descended through the briefed floor, and the IP took control to reposition and re-orient the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a slow and interrupted cross-check between lead aircraft and own instruments, did not keep track of what was happening in own aircraft while flying position. Orientation with respect to the field, the area boundary and the other flight members was re-established only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The corrections were applied late and the resulting excursions reached the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a scan that narrowed onto lead aircraft during the maneuvering, delayed the detection of developing altitude and fuel trends in own aircraft. SP recognized the omission without prompting, restored the alternation between lead, the instruments and the outside references and re-established orientation with respect to the field and the assigned area. The deviation stayed short of the standard limit and required no IP input.
texts.3: SP correlated continuously what was happening on the ground, in own aircraft and in the other flight members, alternating the scan between lead, the control and performance instruments and the outside references. Orientation with respect to the field, the assigned area and the traffic remained accurate, and the mission impact of each event was handled as it appeared.
texts.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted alternation between lead aircraft, own instruments and the outside references and continuously correlated flight position, fuel state and traffic. Adverse factors such as weather, airspace restrictions and traffic density were identified early and their effect on the formation was minimized before it degraded the mission. Orientation was never in doubt at any point of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP kept orientation and stayed within the required standards, but the scan narrowed onto lead aircraft each time position keeping became demanding, and own instruments were checked only after the position was stabilized. The trend was toward monitoring lead at the expense of own aircraft state. SP is expected to keep own control and performance instruments inside the scan while flying position.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the cross-check with the IP calling the own aircraft state when the scan had narrowed onto lead aircraft. Alternating the scan between lead, the instruments and the outside references is still new at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin the alternation without the IP's calls.
texts_at.1: SP re-established orientation with respect to the field, the area boundary and the other flight members, though the re-establishment followed only once IP issued repeated verbal prompting, with the corrections applied late and the resulting excursions reaching the limit of the acceptable standard. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep track of the own aircraft state while flying position, before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP kept orientation and alternated the scan between lead, the instruments and the outside references, restoring without prompting a scan that tended to narrow onto lead during demanding position keeping. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to keep the alternation running through the maneuvering, so the trend in own altitude and fuel is not delayed in the first place.
texts_at.3: SP kept orientation and stayed within the required standards, though the scan narrowed onto lead aircraft each time position keeping became demanding, and own instruments were checked only after the position was stabilized, showing a trend toward monitoring lead at the expense of own aircraft state. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to keep own control and performance instruments inside the scan while flying position.

texts_above.1: SP re-established orientation with respect to the field, the area boundary and the other flight members, though the corrections were first applied late and the resulting excursions reached the limit of the acceptable standard. The re-establishment followed repeated verbal prompting from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP restored the alternation between lead, the instruments and the outside references without prompting whenever the scan narrowed onto lead, and re-established orientation with respect to the field and the assigned area before any excursion developed. Keeping the alternation running through demanding position keeping would remove the delayed detection entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound recovery of the instrument cross-check during demanding position keeping.
texts_above.3: SP correlated continuously what was happening on the ground, in own aircraft and in the other flight members, alternating the scan between lead, the control and performance instruments and the outside references, with orientation with respect to the field, the assigned area and the traffic remaining accurate and the mission impact of each event handled as it appeared. The only refinement left is to hold the same alternation through an extended period of demanding position keeping. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed cross-check discipline through the sortie.
texts_above.4: SP maintained an uninterrupted alternation between lead aircraft, own instruments and the outside references and continuously correlated flight position, fuel state and traffic, with adverse factors such as weather, airspace restrictions and traffic density identified early and their effect on the formation minimized before it degraded the mission, so orientation was never in doubt at any point of the sortie. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exceptional early identification of adverse factors before they affected the mission.

error_modes.label: RISK MANAGEMENT AND DECISION MAKING WITHIN THE FLIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to a decision taken before the available weather, traffic and fuel data had been gathered, committed to the formation profile without identifying its contingencies. No alternative was considered, no decision was stated to the flight and the briefed decision points were passed without a decision. The profile reached a position in which its margins were gone, and the IP had to take control to restore them.
texts.1: SP, due to incomplete gathering of the available data, identified the limiting factor in the profile late and did not state a clear decision or its rationale to the flight. The alternative course of action was adopted only after the IP prompted it verbally and repeated the prompt. The profile stayed safe, but its margins were at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial assessment based on partial information, delayed the decision to alter the profile at a briefed decision point. SP then gathered the missing data, identified the alternative, stated the decision to the flight with its rationale and regulated the flight path accordingly. The margins were preserved and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered the available data before deciding, stated the decisions clearly to the flight and gave the rationale when asked. Actual and potential hazards were recognized and the flight path was regulated so that they were positively avoided.
texts.4: SP identified the contingencies of each phase before they became relevant and had the alternatives ready with their decision points already defined. Decisions were stated to the flight early, concisely and with a rationale that lead could act on immediately. Every hazard was avoided by a wide margin with no degradation of the briefed profile.
texts.marginal: SP identified the hazards and reached correct decisions, but the decisions were formed late and were stated to the flight without the supporting rationale. The trend was toward deciding once the hazard was established rather than at the planned decision point. SP is expected to define the alternatives in advance and to state both the decision and its reason to the flight.

texts_at.0: SP practiced risk management within the flight with the IP prompting the alternative course of action at each decision point, the habit of stating a decision and its rationale to the flight unprompted being new at this stage. The maneuver is being introduced at this point of the syllabus, so no independent standard is required yet. SP is expected to state the first decision of the sortie to the flight without the IP's prompt.
texts_at.1: SP adopted the alternative course of action right at the limit of the standard, the decision following only once the IP prompted it and repeated the prompt. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to gather the data and state the decision with its rationale before the decision point, so the prompt is not needed on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP gathered the available data and stated the decisions to the flight with their rationale, correcting without prompting an initial assessment that rested on partial information. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to gather the missing data as soon as a decision point approaches, so the decision is not delayed.
texts_at.3: SP identified the contingencies, reached correct decisions and regulated the flight path accordingly, with the rationale given to the flight a little after the decision on some occasions. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus. SP is expected to state the decision and its reason together.

texts_above.1: SP identified the contingencies of the profile and gathered the available data, with one decision adopted after a verbal call from the IP. The remaining decisions were stated to the flight at their decision points. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP gathered the missing data without prompting, identified the alternative, stated the decision to the flight with its rationale and regulated the flight path so that the margins were preserved. Gathering that data as soon as the decision point approached would remove the delay entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid recovery of the decision once the missing data was gathered.
texts_above.3: SP identified contingencies and alternatives accurately, gathered the available data before deciding and stated the decisions clearly to the flight, giving the rationale when asked. Actual and potential hazards were recognized and the flight path regulated so that they were positively avoided. The only refinement left is to hold the same rigor when two hazards develop close together. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed decision discipline through the sortie.
texts_above.4: SP identified the contingencies of each phase before they became relevant and had the alternatives ready with their decision points already defined, stating each decision to the flight early, concisely and with a rationale lead could act on at once. Every hazard was avoided by a wide margin with no degradation of the briefed profile. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to outstanding advance definition of decision points before the hazards became relevant.

error_modes.label: TASK PRIORITIZATION AND SATURATION UNDER FORMATION WORKLOAD

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on holding the fingertip picture, dropped every other task while the workload increased. Radio calls, checks and the fuel check were omitted, and the tasks that were attempted were carried out in an order that violated the briefed sequence. Channelized attention on lead wingtip left the aircraft state unmonitored until the IP took control and re-established the flight.
texts.1: SP, due to attention captured by position keeping, handled the tasks one at a time and left the remainder pending as the workload built up. Missing radio calls and checks were completed only after the IP prompted each of them individually. The sequence was recovered late and the accumulated task backlog brought the sortie to the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to attention concentrated on the position picture during the rejoin, delayed the secondary tasks and let two of them accumulate. SP recognized the developing saturation without prompting, re-ordered the tasks by significance and cleared the backlog before the next event. No task was ultimately dropped and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP put the tasks in order of significance without missing anything and without violating any rule, and handled multiple tasks in sequence while flying position. Task management remained deliberate as the workload increased and at no point developed into channelized attention on a single item.
texts.4: SP sequenced the flying, the checks, the radio and the visual scan so that each task was completed at its most efficient point and nothing accumulated. Task loading was distributed ahead of the busy phases, leaving spare capacity available at the rejoin and in the recovery. Attention was never captured by any single item, including the position picture itself.
texts.marginal: SP completed all the tasks in the correct order and inside the standards, but the ordering was reactive and secondary tasks were deferred each time position keeping demanded attention. The trend was toward a backlog that had to be cleared in the quiet phases. SP is expected to sequence the tasks ahead of the busy phases and to keep capacity in reserve for the rejoin.

texts_at.0: SP practiced task prioritization with the IP prompting each missing radio call and check individually. Re-ordering the tasks by significance without prompting is still new at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to begin re-ordering the tasks without the IP's prompts.
texts_at.1: SP completed the missing radio calls and checks and recovered the sequence, though each item followed only once IP prompted it individually, with the sequence recovered late and the accumulated task backlog bringing the sortie to the limit of the acceptable standard. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to re-order the tasks by significance without the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP completed the secondary tasks inside the standard while holding position, clearing without prompting the occasional backlog that built when attention concentrated on the position picture during the rejoin. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to re-order the tasks as soon as two accumulate rather than waiting for the position picture to settle.
texts_at.3: SP completed all the tasks in the correct order and inside the standards, though the ordering was reactive and secondary tasks were deferred each time position keeping demanded attention, with a trend toward a backlog that had to be cleared in the quiet phases. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to sequence the tasks ahead of the busy phases and to keep capacity in reserve for the rejoin.

texts_above.1: SP completed the missing radio calls and checks and recovered the sequence, though each item first followed only once prompted individually, with the sequence recovered late. Each completion followed a verbal prompt from the IP. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP recognized a developing backlog of secondary tasks without prompting, re-ordered the tasks by significance and cleared it before the next event, so that no task was dropped. Re-ordering the tasks as soon as two accumulate would remove the backlog before it forms. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady recovery of the task backlog before the next event.
texts_above.3: SP put the tasks in order of significance without missing anything and without violating any rule, handling multiple tasks in sequence while flying position, with task management remaining deliberate as the workload increased and at no point developing into channelized attention on a single item. The only refinement left is to hold the same order into a longer busy phase. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate task sequencing through the workload increase.
texts_above.4: SP sequenced the flying, the checks, the radio and the visual scan so each task was completed at its most efficient point and nothing accumulated, with task loading distributed ahead of the busy phases, leaving spare capacity available at the rejoin and in the recovery, and attention never captured by any single item, including the position picture itself. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to exemplary distribution of task loading ahead of every busy phase.

error_modes.label: FLEXIBILITY AND CAPACITY - MISSION ADJUSTMENT AND USE OF AVAILABLE RESOURCES

texts.0: SP, due to a lack of assertiveness in stating unable when the flight profile exceeded own capability, continued to accept maneuvers that could no longer be flown safely in position. No alternative course of action was selected to reduce task loading, no knock-it-off was called and the remaining fuel and area were not taken into account. The aircraft was flown beyond SP capacity to control it in formation and the IP took control.
texts.1: SP, due to reluctance to state a limitation to the flight, adjusted the mission only after the IP directed it verbally. The remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area were not used efficiently and the profile was reorganized late in the sortie. Mission effectiveness was preserved only at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation in requesting a reduction of the profile as the conditions changed, continued at a task loading that was close to own capacity. SP then assessed the factors correctly, selected an alternative course of action and stated it to the flight in time, adjusting the remaining events to the available fuel and area. Mission effectiveness was maintained with no IP input.
texts.3: SP coped with the changing conditions of the sortie and adjusted the profile as needed to obtain the briefed objectives, remaining aware of how much task loading could be accepted safely. The remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area were used efficiently, and an alternative course of action was selected whenever it reduced the task loading.
texts.4: SP recognized the change of conditions before it affected the flight and reorganized the remaining profile so that the objectives were obtained within the available fuel, time and area. Own capacity was managed with a clear margin, and limitations and requests were stated to the flight early and without hesitation. No event was flown at the edge of SP capability.
texts.marginal: SP adjusted the mission correctly and never exceeded own capability, but the alternatives were selected late and the limitations were voiced only once the workload had already peaked. The trend was toward absorbing the task loading rather than reducing it. SP is expected to state the limitation and select the alternative at the point it is recognized, not after it becomes pressing.

texts_at.0: SP practiced adjusting the mission with the IP directing the adjustment when the profile had exceeded the current capacity. Stating a limitation to the flight before it becomes pressing is still new at this stage. The Training Section still expects IP assistance for this maneuver at this point. SP is expected to begin stating the limitation without the IP's direction.
texts_at.1: SP adjusted the mission and reorganized the remaining profile, though the adjustment followed only once IP directed it verbally, with the remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area not used efficiently and the profile reorganized late in the sortie. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to state the limitation before the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP adjusted the mission and stated a reduction of the profile to the flight, correcting without prompting a tendency to continue at a task loading close to the own capacity after the conditions changed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to request the reduction as soon as the conditions change, rather than continuing at the higher task loading first.
texts_at.3: SP adjusted the mission correctly and never exceeded the own capability, though the alternatives were selected late and the limitations were voiced only once the workload had already peaked, with a trend toward absorbing the task loading rather than reducing it. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to state the limitation and select the alternative at the point it is recognized, not after it becomes pressing.

texts_above.1: SP adjusted the mission and reorganized the remaining profile, though the adjustment first followed only once directed verbally, with the remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area not used efficiently. The adjustment followed a verbal direction from the IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section at this stage of training.
texts_above.2: SP assessed the factors correctly, selected an alternative course of action and stated it to the flight in time, adjusting the remaining events to the available fuel and area with no prompting from the IP. Requesting the reduction as soon as the conditions change would remove the period at higher task loading entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable recovery of the task loading once the conditions were reassessed.
texts_above.3: SP coped with the changing conditions of the sortie and adjusted the profile as needed to obtain the briefed objectives, remaining aware of how much task loading could be accepted safely, with the remaining flight time, fuel and assigned area used efficiently and an alternative course of action selected whenever it reduced the task loading. The only refinement left is to hold the same awareness through a second, unrelated change of conditions. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good awareness of task loading through the changing conditions.
texts_above.4: SP recognized the change of conditions before it affected the flight and reorganized the remaining profile so the objectives were obtained within the available fuel, time and area, with the own capacity managed with a clear margin and limitations and requests stated to the flight early and without hesitation, so no event was flown at the edge of the own capability. This is beyond what the Training Section asks for at this stage, due to superior anticipation that kept every event well inside the own capability.

error_modes.label: FLIGHT DISCIPLINE, CHECKS AND SOP COMPLIANCE

texts.0: SP, due to an incomplete knowledge of the rules and procedures governing the formation sortie, did not carry out the operational checks in accordance with the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs. Required steps were performed out of order and briefed restrictions of the flight were exceeded. Recovery to base was not managed by SP and the IP took control and completed the procedures and the return to the field.
texts.1: SP, due to a superficial knowledge of the applicable procedures, performed the checks incompletely and out of the published order. Each omission was identified and corrected only after the IP prompted it, and the recovery was flown under continuous IP direction. The procedures were eventually completed, but at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an interruption of the checklist flow while holding position, omitted one step of an operational check and delayed a briefed procedure. SP detected the omission without prompting, restarted the check from the correct point and completed the sequence in the published order. The recovery to base was flown correctly and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP performed all operational checks in accordance with the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs, and carried out the required steps of each procedure in the proper order. Rules and briefed restrictions were respected throughout and the return to base was managed with minimum IP supervision.
texts.4: SP applied the checklist, the Techniques and Procedures Manual and the SOPs precisely and in the correct order at every phase, integrating them with the position keeping without any interruption of the flow. Knowledge of the rules and of the briefed restrictions was complete and applied without hesitation. The recovery to base was planned and executed independently, with no IP supervision required.
texts.marginal: SP completed all the checks and followed the published procedures, but items were occasionally performed out of the normal order and one check was started later than the planned point. The trend was toward fitting the procedures around the position keeping rather than planning them into the sequence. SP is expected to protect the checklist flow and to run each procedure at its briefed point.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the operational checks with the IP prompting each omission and directing the recovery. Performing the checks in the published order without prompting is still new at this stage. The Training Section introduces this maneuver at this point and does not yet ask for an independent standard. SP is expected to begin performing the checks in order without the IP's prompts.
texts_at.1: SP eventually completed the procedures, though each omission was identified and corrected only once IP prompted it, with the recovery flown under continuous IP direction and the procedures completed at the limit of the acceptable standard. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to perform the checks in the published order without the verbal prompt on the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP carried out the operational checks in the published order and restarted without prompting a check that had lost a step to an interruption of the checklist flow while holding position. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to protect the checklist flow through the interruption, so the restart is not needed.
texts_at.3: SP completed all the checks and followed the published procedures within standard, though items were occasionally performed out of the normal order and one check was started later than the planned point, with a trend toward fitting the procedures around the position keeping rather than planning them into the sequence. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to protect the checklist flow and to run each procedure at its briefed point.

texts_above.1: SP eventually completed the procedures, though each omission was first identified and corrected only once prompted, with the recovery flown under continuous IP direction. Each correction followed a verbal prompt from the IP. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus.
texts_above.2: SP detected an omitted step in an operational check without prompting, restarted the check from the correct point and completed the sequence in the published order, with the recovery to base flown correctly. Protecting the checklist flow through the interruption would remove the restart entirely. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured recovery of the checklist flow after an interruption.

The only refinement left is to hold the same order through a second, closely following interruption. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise checklist sequencing maintained through the sortie.

error_modes.label: AGSM AS A CONTINUUM - STRAIN ONSET, INTENSITY AND BREATHING CYCLE

texts.0: SP, due to an anti-G straining maneuver started after the onset of G forces instead of before it, entered the high-G rejoin with no strain established and then held the strain for more than 3 seconds without breathing. Gray out developed at about 4 Gs and SP did not return to 1 G flight to reapply the strain. The IP took control, unloaded the aircraft and terminated all high-G maneuvering for the remainder of the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to a strain applied at a fixed intensity rather than increased as the G increased, lost the leg, abdomen and chest contraction each time the loading built past 3 Gs. The IP had to call for the strain and for the breathing cycle before every high-G maneuver. Vision degraded briefly on two occasions and the required strain was produced only after verbal direction, leaving the AGSM at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a breathing cycle stretched beyond the 2 to 3 second interval during the first high-G turn, allowed the strain to become a single long hold. SP recognized the loss of G tolerance, returned to 1 G flight, reapplied the strain and re-entered the maneuver with full muscle contraction and constant breathing cycles. No vision degradation followed and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP started the AGSM before the onset of G forces and maintained it throughout the period of increased G loading, contracting legs, abdomen and chest and increasing the intensity of the strain as the G increased. Breathing was maintained at approximately every 2 to 3 seconds and no strain was held longer than 3 seconds without breathing. The lower-G segments were flown with all elements of the full AGSM at reduced intensity.
texts.4: SP treated the AGSM as a continuum for the whole sortie, setting the strain before every G onset and modulating its intensity with the loading without any break in the breathing cycle. Full muscle contraction and constant breathing cycles were held through the highest loadings of the profile, and the lower-G segments still received every element of the maneuver. No vision symptom of any degree occurred at any point.
texts.marginal: SP maintained an effective AGSM within the required standard, but the strain was set at the same intensity for every maneuver and the breathing cycle lengthened toward the end of each high-G turn. The trend was toward a fixed strain rather than one that follows the G continuum. SP is expected to increase the intensity of the strain with the loading and to keep breathing at approximately every 2 to 3 seconds.

texts_at.0: SP practiced the AGSM with the IP calling the strain and the breathing cycle before every high-G maneuver. Increasing the strain intensity with the G loading is still new at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to begin increasing the strain intensity without the IP's calls.

error_modes.label: ADVERSE FACTORS AND RETURN OR ALTERNATE READINESS OF THE FLIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to lack of awareness of the published restrictions that were available in the briefing material, flew the formation profile without the weather, the airspace restrictions or the alternate airfield in mind. The area boundaries and the return route for the flight were not known when asked, and no allowance was made for them in own positioning. The IP had to take control to keep the flight inside its area and to direct the return to base.
texts.1: SP, due to an incomplete review of the restrictions in the briefing material, knew the area and the return route for the flight only in outline. The alternate airfield and its weather were recalled correctly only after repeated verbal prompting by the IP. The effect of those factors on own position keeping was recognized late, at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a hurried read of the briefing material, initially quoted the return route for the flight without allowing for one published area restriction. SP noticed the gap against the FLIP data without prompting, restated the route and kept own position keeping consistent with it. The effect on the flight was small and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP kept track of the weather, the airspace and approach restrictions, the traffic density and the return arrangements of the flight while flying position, and minimized the effect of those factors on the mission. The alternate airfield and the route to it were known and stated without prompting.
texts.4: SP held the weather, the restrictions, the traffic picture and the return and alternate arrangements of the flight continuously current while flying position, and passed what mattered to No1 with short standard calls. Adverse factors never reached the mission.
texts.marginal: SP respected the restrictions and kept the flight inside its area, but the alternate airfield and the return route were stated only when the IP asked for them. The trend was toward knowing the restrictions without keeping them current. SP is expected to review the FLIP restrictions and the briefed alternate before the sortie and to restate them as the flight moves.

texts_at.0: SP followed the awareness of the weather, the restrictions and the return arrangements of the flight with the IP naming each factor and the alternate, the habit of holding them while flying position being new at this stage. This is the level of assistance the Training Section still provides at this stage. SP is expected to name the return route and the alternate unprompted before the formation work on the next sortie.
texts_at.1: SP kept awareness of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the return arrangements of the flight inside the code 1 band, the alternate airfield stated only after the IP prompted it. texts_at.2: SP kept awareness of the weather, the airspace restrictions and the return arrangements of the flight, correcting without prompting a return route first quoted without one published restriction. texts_at.3: SP held the weather, the area restrictions, the traffic density and the return and alternate arrangements of the flight in mind throughout the sortie, with the alternate's weather refreshed a little later than the other factors. Reading the published restrictions against the route before stating it would remove even that correction. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to sure-handed awareness of adverse factors across the flight.
texts_above.4: SP kept the weather, the restrictions, the traffic picture and the return and alternate arrangements of the flight continuously current while flying position, passing relevant changes to No1 with short standard calls. The effect of adverse factors on the formation was minimized before it reached the mission. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior awareness of the operating environment of the flight.

error_modes.label: AGSM DEMONSTRATION AND PERSONAL G-TOLERANCE - BUILD-UP, CYCLE LENGTH AND INFORMING THE OTHER CREW-MEMBER

texts.0: SP, due to a demonstration flown at a single high G-level instead of a gradual build, made no assessment of personal G-tolerance before the formation profile. The turns were too short for a proper AGSM cycle, no break between turns was used for critique and rest, and SP did not tell the IP that the demonstration was approaching personal limits. The IP stopped the demonstration, took control and terminated the high-G work.
texts.1: SP, due to turns held for less than the 10 to 15 seconds of a full AGSM cycle, completed the demonstration without the 4 to 5 breathing cycles needed for a proper assessment. The G-level was stepped up only after the IP called for it, and the approach to personal tolerance was reported only when the IP asked. The demonstration was completed at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to starting the demonstration at a higher G-level than the build-up called for, shortened the first turn and left too little time for a proper AGSM cycle. SP recognized this, rebuilt the series from 2 Gs toward 4 Gs as proficiency allowed, used the break between turns for critique and rest and told the IP when personal tolerance was approached. No IP input was required.
texts.3: SP flew the AGSM demonstration as a series of turns at gradually increasing G-levels from 2 Gs toward 4 Gs, each long enough for a full AGSM cycle of 10 to 15 seconds with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles. The breaks were used for critique and rest, and the other crew-member was informed when personal G-tolerance was approached.
texts.4: SP built the demonstration in small steps matched to proficiency, held every cycle to its full duration and reported own G-tolerance limits clearly before the high-G formation work. Fitness, rest and hydration had been prepared in advance.
texts.marginal: SP completed the demonstration within the standard, but the turns ended close to the minimum cycle length and the report on personal tolerance came only when the IP asked. The trend was toward treating the demonstration as a formality. SP is expected to hold each cycle to its full length and to report the approach to personal G-tolerance without being asked.

texts_at.0: SP followed the AGSM demonstration with the IP calling each G-level and the break between turns, the habit of reporting the approach to personal G-tolerance unprompted being new at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to report the approach to personal tolerance before the IP asks on the next demonstration.
texts_at.1: SP flew the AGSM demonstration at the outer edge of the standard, the cycles of 10 to 15 seconds held to their full duration only after the IP called for them. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to hold every turn for the full cycle with at least 4 to 5 breathing cycles, so the IP does not need to call the duration.
texts_at.2: SP flew the AGSM demonstration as a series of turns at rising G-levels, correcting without prompting a first turn that had been kept too short for a full cycle. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to plan the length of each turn from the start, so every cycle reaches 10 to 15 seconds.
texts_at.3: SP flew the demonstration as a gradual build from 2 Gs toward 4 Gs with a break for critique and rest between turns and breathing cycles throughout, with one cycle ending a little short of the planned length. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to hold that cycle to the full 10 to 15 seconds as well.

error_modes.label: FLIGHT DISCIPLINE FROM PREPARATION TO DEBRIEF - THE FLIGHT LEADER'S DIRECTIVES AND THE BRIEFED CONTRACT
error_modes.source: technique:9.1 INTRODUCTION - PURPOSE, FLIGHT DISCIPLINE, AGGRESSIVENESS

texts.0: SP, due to preparation that skipped the flight rules, the unit standards and the formation sections of the manual, arrived unprepared to brief the formation. Questions on the formation profile at the briefing were left unanswered and the briefed restrictions were not known before engine start. The sortie was flown without the briefed contract and the IP had to take control to bring the execution back inside the governing guidelines.
texts.1: SP, due to a study of the profile that did not extend to the flight rules and the unit standards, could state the formation plan but not the restrictions and standards around it. Several briefed points were understood only after the IP or No1 repeated them in flight. The execution followed the brief at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a preparation gap on one briefed restriction, initially flew one phase differently from the pre-flight briefing. SP noticed the difference against the briefing notes without prompting, stated it and returned to the briefed execution. The flight leader's later directives were followed as given and no IP input was required.
texts.3: SP arrived prepared, was ready to discuss the formation plan and executed the sortie as briefed in accordance with the governing guidelines, following every real-time alteration directed by the flight leader. The debrief addressed flight discipline.
texts.4: SP prepared to a depth at which the formation profile, its restrictions and their reasons could be briefed from memory, flew the sortie exactly as briefed and answered every directive of the flight leader at once. Flight discipline was assessed by SP in the debrief before the IP raised it.
texts.marginal: SP prepared and executed the formation sortie as briefed and followed the directives of the flight leader, but the flight rules and unit standards were known less thoroughly than the profile and one restriction needed a second look at the briefing. The trend was toward preparing the profile first and the standards second. SP is expected to give the flight rules and the unit standards equal preparation time.

texts_at.0: SP followed the preparation, the briefing and the execution of the formation sortie with the IP restating the governing guidelines in flight, the habit of working from them unaided being new at this stage. Performance is consistent with a first exposure at this point of the syllabus, where the Training Section still provides assistance. SP is expected to state the main briefed restrictions before the IP asks at the next briefing.
texts_at.1: SP prepared and executed the formation sortie as briefed just inside the standard, several restrictions becoming clear only after they were repeated in flight. Performance met the desired standard for this stage. SP is expected to study the flight rules and the unit standards to the same depth as the profile, as Techniques and Procedures Manual 9.1 describes, so none needs repeating in the air.
texts_at.2: SP prepared and executed the formation sortie as briefed and followed the directives of the flight leader, correcting without prompting one phase first flown differently from the briefing. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training. SP is expected to close each preparation gap before the briefing, so no phase departs from it.
texts_at.3: SP arrived prepared, was ready to discuss the formation plan and executed the sortie as briefed with every real-time alteration from the flight leader followed, with one debrief point recognized a moment after it was raised. The standard for the Training Section was met. SP is expected to recognize each debrief point before it is raised.

texts_above.1: SP prepared and executed the formation sortie as briefed, with one briefed restriction repeated after a verbal call from the IP. All the other points followed the briefing unprompted. This is above the level the Training Section requires at this point.
texts_above.2: SP found the departure from the briefing against its own notes without prompting, stated it and returned to the briefed execution for the rest of the sortie. Closing that preparation gap before the briefing would remove even that departure. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound preparation for the formation briefing.
texts_above.3: SP knew the flight rules, the unit standards and the formation sections of the manual, was on time and ready to discuss the plan, answered every question at the briefing and followed each real-time alteration from the flight leader. The debrief was used to evaluate flight discipline. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed adherence to the briefed contract.
texts_above.4: SP prepared to a depth at which the formation profile, its restrictions and their reasons could be briefed from memory, then flew the sortie exactly as briefed and responded to every directive from the flight leader smoothly and at once. The debrief of flight discipline began with SP's own assessment. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding adherence to the formation contract.
